args.text: [lane-wren] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to old servers after a site moves or fails over, causing errors or outages. (2) Slow recovery from attacks: a poisoned or hijacked answer stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting people until it expires. (3) Delayed changes: security fixes, certificate moves or traffic shifts take longer to reach everyone, so rollouts are unpredictable.

[lane-wren] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If repeating the request gives the same result as sending it once, a retry cannot cause double charges, duplicate records or other unwanted side effects.

[lane-wren] UUIDv7 (a version of Universally Unique Identifier that starts with a timestamp) has two trade-offs as a primary key. (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, bigger than a plain whole-number key, so indexes and related tables grow and use more memory. (2) Leaked timing: because the creation time is built into the value, anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the record was made, and ordering within the same millisecond is not guaranteed unless extra care is taken.

[lane-wren] A write-ahead log is a record of intended changes that a database saves to durable storage before it changes the main data files. If the system crashes part-way through, it can replay or discard the logged changes on restart, so no committed work is lost and the data is not left half-written.

[lane-wren] (1) Fair comparison: a new client version may change speed, defaults or retry behaviour, so results from different versions would measure the client rather than the system under test. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the benchmark later and get comparable numbers, and any change in results can be traced to a deliberate change, not a silent upgrade.

[lane-wren] Backpressure is a way for a queue to signal producers to slow down, pause or stop sending when it is filling faster than consumers can empty it. This keeps the queue from growing without limit, which would otherwise use up memory, add long delays or cause crashes.

[lane-wren] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) the same job is scheduled on more than one machine, so each one starts it; (2) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled start arrives, so the two overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, for example a lock file or a database lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-wren] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item, saying that the item was removed and when. Replicas need it because, without it, a copy that missed the deletion would look like the newest holder of the data and could bring the item back. Tombstones are cleared away after a set time, once every copy has seen them.

[lane-wren] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs, so re-running it often gives a different result; (2) the failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, test order, shared data or the machine it runs on, and they usually vanish when the test is run alone. A truly failing test fails every time until the code is fixed.

[lane-wren] A lease-based lock gives a holder the lock for a set length of time, and each machine judges that time by its own clock. If the holder's clock runs slow, it thinks it still has the lock after the lock service has already given it to someone else. Two holders then work at once, which is the very thing the lock should prevent. Fencing tokens (numbers that rise with each new lease) help the shared resource reject the older holder.
